With these words he cried out with a great voice, “Lazarus, here, outside!”
The dead man came out with strips of linen wrapped around his hands and feet, and a cloth around his face. Jesus told them, “Untie him and let him go.”
So, many of the Jews who had come to visit Mary, and who had watched what he did, put their faith in him.
But some of them went off to the Pharisees and told them what Jesus had done.
The chief priests and the Pharisees therefore convened the council{i} and said, “What are we doing? Here is this man working many signs.
If we let him go on like this, everyone will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away both our place{j} and our nation.”
But one of them, Caiaphas,{k} who was high priest that year, said to them, “You know nothing at all,
nor do you consider that it is to your advantage for one man to die on behalf of the people, rather than for the entire nation to be lost.”
It was not from himself that he said this; rather, as high priest that year he prophesied that Jesus would die on behalf of the nation,
and not for the nation only, but also to gather into one the scattered children of God.
From that day, then, their counsel was to put him to death.
For this reason Jesus no longer walked about in public among the Jews. He left that place for the country close to the wilderness, to a town called Ephraim,{l} and stayed there with the disciples.
Now the Passover of the Jews was near, and many went up from the countryside to Jerusalem before the Passover to purify themselves.
They searched for Jesus, and as they stood in the temple they asked one another, “What do you think? Will he not come to the festival at all?”
Now the chief priests and the Pharisees had given orders that anyone who knew where he was should report it, so that they might arrest him.

notes.text: Lazarus: a Greek form of Hebrew *Eleazar*, “God has helped.”
Mary: Greek *Mariam* or *Maria*, from Hebrew *Miryam* (Miriam), a name of uncertain meaning.
Martha: Aramaic, “lady” or “mistress.”
The anointing is narrated in 12:1–8; John refers to it here as already known to his readers.
Thomas … the Twin: *Thomas* is from Aramaic *toma*, “twin,” and Greek *Didymos* also means “twin.”
Less than two miles: literally “about fifteen stadia,” about 1¾ miles (2.8 km).
I am the resurrection and the life: the fifth “I am” saying with a predicate (see the note on 6:20). P45 and a few other witnesses are reported to omit “and the life.”

Deeply moved in spirit: Greek *enebrimēsato*, a strong word that elsewhere expresses indignation or stern rebuke (Mark 1:43; 14:5); here perhaps anger at the power of death, or intense distress. So also in 11:38.
Council: Greek *synedrion*, the Sanhedrin, the supreme Jewish council in Jerusalem, presided over by the high priest.
Our place: probably the temple (compare Acts 6:13–14), or perhaps Jerusalem or the council’s position.
Caiaphas: Joseph Caiaphas, high priest AD 18–36, son-in-law of Annas (18:13). *That year* means “in that fateful year.”
Ephraim: perhaps et-Taiyibeh, about 12 miles (19 km) northeast of Jerusalem. The name means “doubly fruitful” (Gen 41:52).

verses.text: Six days before the Passover Jesus came to Bethany, where Lazarus was, whom Jesus had raised from the dead.
There they gave a dinner for him. Martha was serving, and Lazarus was one of those reclining at table with him.
Then Mary took a pound{a} of very costly perfume, pure nard,{b} anointed Jesus’ feet, and wiped his feet with her hair; and the house was filled with the fragrance of the perfume.
But Judas Iscariot, one of his disciples, who was about to betray him, says,
“Why was this ointment not sold for three hundred days’ wages,{c} and the proceeds given to the poor?”
He said this not because he cared about the poor, but because he was a thief; he kept the money bag and used to help himself to what was put in it.
So Jesus said, “Let her alone; she was to keep it for the day of my burial.{d}
For you always have the poor with you, but you do not always have me.”
Then a large crowd of the Jews found out he was there, and they came, not for Jesus’ sake alone, but to see Lazarus too, whom he had raised from the dead.
The chief priests, however, resolved to kill Lazarus also,
because many of the Jews were leaving them for his sake and putting their faith in Jesus.
On the following day the large crowd who had come up for the feast, hearing that Jesus was on his way into Jerusalem,
So they took branches of palm trees and went out to meet him, shouting, “Hosanna!{e} Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord,{f} even the King of Israel!”
Jesus came upon a young donkey and seated himself on it, just as Scripture says,
“Fear not, daughter of Zion; look, your king comes, sitting on the colt of a donkey.”{g}
His disciples did not grasp this at first. Only after Jesus had been glorified did they remember that these things were written about him, and that these were the things people had done to him.
The crowd that had been with him when he called Lazarus out of the tomb and raised him from the dead kept bearing witness.
That was the reason the crowd went to meet him: they had heard that he had performed this sign.
So the Pharisees said to one another, “You see, you are getting nowhere. Look, the world has gone after him!”
Among those who went up to worship at the festival were some Greeks.
They approached Philip, who was from Bethsaida in Galilee, and made a request of him: “Sir, we wish to see Jesus.”
Philip goes and tells Andrew; Andrew and Philip go and tell Jesus.
And Jesus answers them, “The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified.
Amen, amen, I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains a single grain; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.
The one who loves his life is losing it, and the one who hates his life in this world will guard it to life eternal.
Whoever serves me must follow me, and my servant will be wherever I am. The Father will honor anyone who serves me.
“Now my soul is in turmoil. What am I to say? ‘Father, rescue me from this hour’? No, this is the very reason I came to this hour.
Father, bring glory to your name.” Then a voice came from heaven: “I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again.”
The crowd standing there heard it and said it had thundered. Others said, “An angel has spoken to him.”
Jesus replied, “It was not on my account that this voice came, but on yours.
Now is the judgment of this world; now the ruler of this world will be driven out.
And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself.”{h}
He said this to indicate by what kind of death he was going to die.
The crowd answered him, “We have heard out of the Law that the Messiah abides forever.{i} So how do you say the Son of Man has to be lifted up? Who is he, this Son of Man?”

Jesus then said to them, “For only a short time more the light is with you. Keep walking as long as you have the light, lest darkness seize you; the one who walks in darkness has no idea where he goes.
Believe in the light while you have it, so that you may become people of the light.” When Jesus had said these things, he left and hid from them.
But for all the signs he had done in their sight, they did not believe in him,
This happened so that the word spoken by the prophet Isaiah would be fulfilled: “Lord, who has believed what we reported? To whom has the Lord’s mighty arm been revealed?”{j}
That is why they could not believe; for again Isaiah said,
“He has made their eyes blind and their heart hard, lest they see with the eyes and grasp with the heart and turn back, and I heal them.”{k}
Isaiah said these things because{l} he saw his glory and spoke about him.
Even so, many of the leaders believed in him. But because of the Pharisees they would not admit it openly, for fear of being expelled from the synagogue,
They loved the glory people give more than the glory God gives.
Then Jesus cried out and said, “Whoever believes in me believes not in me but in the one who sent me.
And whoever sees me sees the one who sent me.
I, a light, have come into the world, that whoever believes in me may not be left in the dark.
If someone hears my sayings and fails to keep them, it is not I who judge him. I came not to condemn the world but to save it.
Whoever sets me aside and will not accept my sayings has one who judges him: the very word I have spoken will be his judge on the last day.
I did not speak from myself; the Father who sent me gave me his own command about what I should say and how I should speak.
And I know that his command is life eternal. So the things I speak, I speak as the Father has said them to me.”

notes.text: A pound: literally “a litra,” the Roman pound (Latin *libra*), about 12 ounces (327 g).
Pure nard: Greek *nardos pistikē*, an aromatic oil made from a plant of the Himalayas; the meaning of *pistikē* is uncertain (perhaps “genuine” or a place name).
Three hundred days’ wages: literally “three hundred denarii,” about a year’s wages for a laborer. See the note on 6:7.

She was to keep it for the day of my burial: the Greek is difficult. Many later manuscripts read “she has kept it for the day of my burial.” Others take it as “Let her keep it for the day of my burial.”
Hosanna: a Greek transliteration of Hebrew *hoshiah na*, “Save, we pray!” (Ps 118:25), which had become a shout of praise.
Ps 118:26. In the Hebrew text, “the Lord” is Yahweh.
Zech 9:9, abbreviated; *do not be afraid* may come from Isa 40:9 or Zeph 3:16. *Zion* is the hill of Jerusalem, and by extension the city and its people.
All people: P66 (as reported), Sinaiticus (first hand), Codex Bezae and the Latin versions read “all things.”
Compare Ps 89:36–37; Isa 9:7; Ezek 37:25; Dan 7:14. *The Law* here means the Scriptures generally.
Isa 53:1, following the Greek Old Testament, which adds the opening “Lord” (addressed to God). In the Hebrew text, “the arm of the Lord” is “the arm of Yahweh.”
Isa 6:10, in a form that differs from both the Hebrew and the Greek Old Testament.
Because: so the Westcott–Hort text with the earliest manuscripts; many later manuscripts read “when.” Isaiah’s vision of the Lord’s glory is in Isa 6:1–5.

verses.text: It was before the feast of the Passover, and Jesus knew that his hour had come to pass out of this world to the Father. He had loved his own who were in the world, and he loved them to the end.{a}
During supper,{b} when the devil had already planted in the heart of Judas son of Simon Iscariot the resolve to hand him over,
Jesus, knowing that the Father had put everything into his hands, and that he had come out from God and was going back to God,
gets up from the supper, lays aside his outer garments, takes a towel, and ties it around his waist.
After that, he poured water into a basin and began washing the disciples’ feet, drying them with the towel wrapped around his waist.
So he comes to Simon Peter, who says to him, “Lord, you, washing my feet?”
Jesus replied, “What I do, you do not understand yet; you will come to know it after these things.”
Peter says to him, “Never shall you wash my feet, not ever!” Jesus answered him, “Unless I wash you, you have no share with me.”
Simon Peter says to him, “Lord, then not only my feet, but my hands and my head as well!”
Jesus says to him, “One who has bathed needs only to wash his feet;{c} he is clean all over. And you are clean, though not all of you.”
He knew his betrayer; that is why he said, “You are not all clean.”
After he had washed their feet, put his outer clothing back on, and returned to his place, he asked them, “Do you understand what I have just done to you?
You call me ‘the Teacher’ and ‘the Lord,’ and you are right to say it, for so I am.
If I then, the Lord and the Teacher, have washed your feet, you too are bound to wash one another’s feet.
I have set you a pattern, so that you also may do as I have done for you.
Amen, amen, I tell you, a slave is not above his master, nor is a messenger{d} above the one who sent him.
Now that you know these things, blessed are you if you act on them.
I am not speaking of all of you; I know whom I have chosen. But the Scripture must be fulfilled: ‘The one who eats my bread has raised his heel against me.’{e}
I tell you this now, ahead of the event, that once it takes place you may believe that I am.{f}
Amen, amen, I tell you, whoever welcomes anyone I send welcomes me, and whoever welcomes me welcomes the one who sent me.”
After saying this, Jesus was troubled in spirit, and he testified, “Amen, amen, I tell you, one of you will betray me.”
The disciples looked at one another, at a loss to know whom he meant.
There was reclining close to Jesus{g} one of his disciples, whom Jesus loved.{h}
So Simon Peter motions to him to ask Jesus whom he was speaking of.
Leaning back, then, against Jesus’ chest, that disciple says to him, “Lord, who is it?”
Jesus replied, “I will dip a piece of bread, and whoever receives it is the one.” Then he dipped the bread and handed it to Judas, the son of Simon Iscariot.
After the morsel, Satan{i} then entered into him. So Jesus says to him, “What you are doing, do quickly.”
But none of those at table knew why he had said this to him.
Since Judas had charge of the money bag, some supposed that Jesus was telling him, “Buy what we need for the feast,” or that he should give something to the poor.
So, after receiving the morsel, he went out at once. And it was night.
When he had gone out, Jesus says, “Now has the Son of Man been glorified, and God has been glorified in him.
And God{j} will glorify him in himself, and without delay.
Little children, only a little while more am I with you. You will seek me; and what I said to the Jews I say now to you as well: ‘Where I go, you are unable to come.’
I am giving you a new commandment: love one another. As I have loved you, so you are to love one another.
By this everyone will recognize that you are my disciples: if you have love among yourselves.”
Simon Peter says to him, “Lord, where are you going?” Jesus answered, “Where I am going you cannot follow me now, but you will follow later.”
Peter says to him, “Lord, why can I not follow you now? I will lay down my life for you.”
Jesus answered, “You will give up your life for me? Truly, truly, I say to you, before the rooster crows, you will have denied me three times.

notes.text: To the end: or “to the uttermost,” “completely”; Greek *eis telos* can mean both.
During supper: so the Westcott–Hort text with Sinaiticus (first hand) and Vaticanus (present participle, as reported); many manuscripts read “when supper was over.”

Needs only to wash his feet: the words “except the feet” (here “only … his feet”) are bracketed in the Westcott–Hort text; Sinaiticus, some Latin witnesses and some early writers lack them, giving “One who has bathed has no need to wash.”
Messenger: Greek *apostolos*, “one who is sent,” the word usually rendered “apostle.”
Ps 41:9 (40:10 Greek). To raise one’s heel against someone is to turn on him in treachery.
That I am: Greek *egō eimi*, perhaps “that I am he”; see the notes on 6:20 and 8:58.
Close to Jesus: literally “in the bosom of Jesus.” At a formal meal the guests reclined on their left side, so that the head of one lay near the chest of the one to his left. Compare 1:18.

Whom Jesus loved: the first mention of the “beloved disciple,” who appears again at 19:26; 20:2; 21:7, 20, and is named as the source of the Gospel at 21:24. He is unnamed in the Gospel; second-century tradition identified him with John the son of Zebedee.
Satan: from Hebrew *satan*, “adversary, accuser.”

God: many manuscripts, followed by most modern editions, begin the verse “If God has been glorified in him, God will also …”; the clause is absent from P66, Sinaiticus (first hand), Vaticanus, Ephraemi (first hand) and Bezae (as reported), and from the Westcott–Hort text.

verses.text: “Do not let your hearts be troubled. You believe in God; believe also in me.{a}
My Father’s house has many dwelling places.{b} Were it otherwise, would I have said to you that I go to prepare you a place?{c}
And when I have gone and prepared a place for you, I will come back and bring you to myself, so that you may be where I am.
And where I am going, you know the way.”{d}
Thomas says to him, “Lord, we have no idea where you are going; how can we know the way?”
Jesus says to him, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life.{e} Nobody comes to the Father except through me.
If you had known me, you would have known my Father also.{f} From now on you know him and have seen him.”
Philip says to him, “Lord, show us the Father, and that will be enough for us.”
Jesus says to him, “Have I been among you all this time, Philip, and still you have not come to know me? Anyone who has seen me has seen the Father. How is it that you say, ‘Show us the Father’?
Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father in me? The sayings I speak to you are not from myself; the Father, who abides in me, is doing his own works.
Take my word for it that I am in the Father and the Father in me; or else believe on the strength of the works themselves.
Truly, truly, I say to you, anyone who believes in me will do the works I do, and will do even greater ones, because I am going to the Father.
Whatever you ask in my name I will do, so that the Father may be glorified in the Son.
If you ask me{g} for anything in my name, I will do it.
“Love me, and you will keep the commands that are mine.
And I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Advocate,{h} to be with you forever:
the Spirit of truth. The world is unable to receive him, for it does not behold him or recognize him; but you recognize him, for he abides beside you and is{i} in you.
I will not leave you orphans; I am coming to you.
Yet a little while, and the world beholds me no more; but you behold me. Because I live, you will live as well.
On that day you will know that I am in my Father, and you in me, and I in you.
Whoever holds my commands and keeps them is the one who loves me. My Father will love the one who loves me, and I will love him and make myself plain to him.”
Judas (not Iscariot){j} says to him, “Lord, what has happened, that you are going to show yourself to us and not to the world?”
Jesus answered him, “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him.
The one without love for me does not keep my sayings; and the word you are hearing is not my own, but belongs to the Father who sent me.
“All this I have told you while still remaining with you.
But the Advocate, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you everything and remind you of everything I have said to you.
Peace I leave you; my peace I give you; I give it not in the way the world gives. Let your hearts not be shaken, nor be fearful.
You heard what I said to you: ‘I go away, and I come to you.’ Had you loved me, you would have been glad that I go to the Father, for the Father is greater than I.
And now I have told you before it happens, so that when it happens you may believe.
I will not say much more to you, because the ruler of this world is approaching. He has no power over me;{k}
but so that the world may know that I love the Father, I do just as the Father has commanded me. Rise, let us go from here.{l}

notes.text: You believe in God; believe also in me: both verbs can be either statements or commands: “Believe in God; believe also in me,” or “You believe in God, and you believe in me.”
Dwelling places: Greek *monai*, “places to stay” (the noun from *menō*, “remain, abide,” as in 14:23); the older rendering “mansions” is from the Latin *mansiones*.
Would I have told you …?: or “If it were not so, I would have told you, for I am going to make ready a place for you.” The punctuation and the presence of “for” (in many manuscripts) are uncertain.
You know the way: many manuscripts read, in effect, “You know where I am going, and you know the way.”
I am the way, and the truth, and the life: the sixth “I am” saying with a predicate (see the note on 6:20).
You would have known my Father also: P66, Sinaiticus and Bezae (as reported) read, in effect, “If you have come to know me, you will also know my Father.”
Me: so the Westcott–Hort text (in brackets) with P66, Sinaiticus and Vaticanus (as reported); many manuscripts lack “me.”

Advocate: Greek *paraklētos*, “one called alongside” to help, used of a legal advocate or counselor; also rendered “Helper,” “Counselor” or “Comforter,” or transliterated “Paraclete.” So in 14:26; 15:26; 16:7; and of Jesus in 1 John 2:1.
Is: so the Westcott–Hort text with P66 (first hand), Vaticanus and Bezae (first hand, as reported); many manuscripts read “will be.”
Judas (not Iscariot): probably the “Judas son of James” of Luke 6:16 and Acts 1:13, perhaps the same as Thaddaeus (Mark 3:18). *Judas* is the Greek form of *Judah*, “praised.”
He has no hold on me: literally “in me he has nothing.”
Rise, let us go from here: the discourse continues through chapters 15–17 before they leave in 18:1; many scholars see here a sign that the farewell discourses were composed in stages.

verses.text: “I am the true vine,{a} and the vinedresser is my Father.
Every branch in me that yields no fruit he cuts away, and every branch that yields fruit he prunes clean,{b} that it may yield fruit more abundantly.
Already you are clean, by reason of the word I have spoken to you.
Abide in me, and I in you. A branch has no power to yield fruit by itself unless it abides in the vine, and no more have you unless you abide in me.
I am the vine; you are the branches. The one abiding in me, with me abiding in him, is the one who yields fruit in plenty; for apart from me you are able to do nothing.
If anyone does not abide in me, he is thrown out like the branch and withers; and such branches are gathered and tossed into the fire, and they burn.
If you abide in me, and my sayings abide in you, ask for whatever you will, and it shall come about for you.
Herein is my Father glorified: that you yield fruit in plenty and so prove to be{c} my disciples.
Just as the Father loved me, so I too loved you. Abide in my love.
If you keep my commands, you will abide in my love, as I have kept the commands of my Father and abide in his love.
I have said all this to you so that my joy may be within you, and your joy brought to fullness.
“This is the command that is mine: love one another as I loved you.
No one has love greater than this, that a person lay down his life on behalf of his friends.
You are friends of mine if you do the things I command you.
I no longer call you slaves, since a slave is not let into his master’s plans. You I have called friends, for everything I heard from my Father I have shared with you.
It was not you who chose me; I chose you, and I appointed you to go out and yield fruit, fruit that will abide, so that the Father may grant you whatever you ask him in my name.
This I command you: love one another.
“If the world hates you, know that it hated me before it hated you.
Were you of the world, the world would be fond of what is its own. But because you are not of the world, but I chose you out from the world, for this reason the world hates you.
Call to mind the word I spoke to you: ‘A slave is not above his master.’{d} Since they persecuted me, they will persecute you also; since they kept my word, they will keep yours as well.{e}
But all these things they will do to you for my name’s sake, because the one who sent me they do not know.
Had I not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin; but as things are, they have no excuse to cover their sin.
Whoever hates me hates my Father as well.
If I had not done among them works that no one else had done, they would not be guilty of sin. But now they have seen those works, and they have hated both me and my Father.
But this happened to fulfill what is written in their Law: ‘They hated me for no reason.’{f}
“When the Advocate{g} comes, whom I will send you from the Father, the Spirit of truth who goes forth from the Father, he will bear witness about me;
and you too are witnesses, for you have been with me from the start.

notes.text: I am the true vine: the seventh “I am” saying with a predicate (see the note on 6:20). In the Old Testament Israel is God’s vine or vineyard (Ps 80:8–16; Isa 5:1–7; Jer 2:21).
Prunes clean: Greek *kathairei*, “cleanses,” a wordplay with *katharoi*, “clean,” in 15:3.
Prove to be: so the Westcott–Hort text (subjunctive, as reported from Vaticanus and Bezae); many manuscripts read “you will be.”
Since … since: or “If … if.” The second clause may be ironic.
Ps 35:19; 69:4 (34:19; 68:5 Greek). *Law* here means the Scriptures generally.
Advocate: Greek *paraklētos*; see the note on 14:16.

verses.text: “All this I have said to you so that you will not be made to stumble.{a}
They will put you out of the synagogues. Indeed, a time is coming when anyone who kills you will suppose he is offering God an act of worship.
And they will do these things because they have known neither the Father nor me.
But I have told you these things so that, when their hour arrives, you may remember that I told you of them. I did not speak of this to you at the beginning, because I was with you.
“But now I go to him who sent me, and none of you asks me, ‘Where are you going?’
Rather, sorrow has filled your hearts because I have spoken of these things.
But it is the truth I tell you: it is to your advantage that I depart. Unless I depart, the Advocate will not come to you; if I go, though, I will send him to you.
And when he comes, he will expose the world’s error{b} concerning sin and righteousness and judgment:
concerning sin, because they do not believe in me;
concerning righteousness, because I go to the Father and you see me no longer;
concerning judgment, because the ruler of this world has been judged.
“I have yet many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now.

When he comes, the Spirit of truth, he will guide you into all the truth;{c} for he will not speak from himself, but will speak whatever he hears, and he will announce to you the things that are coming.
He will bring glory to me, because he will take what is mine and make it known to you.
Everything the Father has belongs to me. That is why I said that he takes what is mine and makes it known to you.
“A little while, and you no longer see me; and again a little while, and you will see me.”

At this, some of his disciples began to say to each other, “Whatever is this he says to us, ‘A little while, and you do not see me, and again a little while, and you will see me,’ and, ‘Because I am going to the Father’?”
So they kept asking, “What is this ‘little while’ he speaks of? We do not know what he means.”

Jesus knew they wanted to ask him something, so he said to them, “Are you discussing with each other what I meant when I said, ‘In a little while you will not see me, and then in a little while you will see me’?
Truly, truly, I say to you, you will cry and mourn while the world celebrates. You will be sorrowful, but your sorrow will become joy.
A woman in labor suffers, because her hour has arrived. But when she has delivered the child, she no longer remembers the pain, in her joy that a human being has been born into the world.
So you also now have grief; but I will see you again, and your hearts will rejoice, and your joy no one takes from you.
On that day you will not ask me anything. Truly, truly, I say to you, whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will give you.{d}
Until now you have asked nothing in my name. Ask, and you will receive, so that your joy may be complete.
“I have spoken these things to you in figures of speech.{e} An hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you in figures, but will tell you plainly about the Father.
On that day you will ask in my name; and I do not say to you that I will ask the Father on your behalf,
for the Father himself loves you, because you have loved me and have believed that I came from the Father.{f}
From the Father I came out, and I have come into the world; now once more I leave the world and make my way to the Father.”
His disciples say, “There! Now you are speaking plainly and using no figure of speech.
Now we can see that you know everything and do not need anyone to ask you questions. Because of this, we believe that you came from God.”
Jesus answered them, “Do you believe now?{g}
See, the hour is coming, and has now come, for you to be scattered each to his own, leaving me by myself. And yet I am not by myself, for the Father is with me.
I have told you these things so that in me you may have peace. In the world you have distress; but take courage: I have conquered the world.”

notes.text: Made to stumble: Greek *skandalizō*, to cause to fall away from faith.
Expose the world’s error: Greek *elenchō*, “convict, prove wrong, bring to light.”
Into all the truth: some manuscripts, including Sinaiticus and Bezae (as reported), read “in all the truth.”

He will give it to you in my name: so the Westcott–Hort text with P5, Sinaiticus, Vaticanus and Ephraemi (as reported); many manuscripts read “whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will give you.”
Figures of speech: Greek *paroimia*, a veiled or enigmatic saying; so in 10:6 and 16:29.
From the Father: so the Westcott–Hort text with Vaticanus and Bezae (as reported, “from the Father,” *para tou patros*); many manuscripts read “from God.”
Do you believe now?: or “Now you believe!”

verses.text: After Jesus said these things, he looked up to heaven and said, “Father, the time has come. Give glory to your Son, so that your Son may give glory to you,
since you gave him authority over all flesh, so that he might give eternal life to all whom you have given him.{a}
And eternal life is this: that they know you, the only true God, and the one you sent, Jesus Christ.
On the earth I have brought you glory, finishing the task you assigned me.
So now, Father, glorify me at your own side with the glory I had at your side before the world existed.
“To those you gave me from the world I have revealed your name.{b} They belonged to you, and you entrusted them to me, and they have held fast to your word.
They know now that all you have given me comes from you;
for the sayings you gave me I have passed on to them, and they took them in and knew in truth that I came forth from you, and they believed that you sent me.
It is for them that I make my request. I do not make it for the world, but for those you have given me, because they are yours.
All that I have is yours, and all that you have is mine. Through them I have been glorified.
I am in the world no longer, but they remain in the world, while I come to you. Holy Father, guard them by your name, the name you have given me,{c} that they may be one as we are one.
When I was with them, I protected them by your name, the name you gave me. I watched over them, and not one was lost except the one headed for destruction,{d} so that Scripture would be fulfilled.
But now I am coming to you, and I speak these things while in the world, so that they may have my joy brought to fullness within themselves.
I have given them your word, and the world hated them, since they are not of the world, as I am not of the world.
My request is not that you take them out of the world, but that you keep them from the evil one.{e}
They are not of the world, as I am not of the world.
Make them holy{f} by the truth; your word is truth.
Just as you sent me into the world, I in turn have sent them into the world.
I set myself apart for their sake, so that they also may be truly set apart.
“Nor do I make request for these alone, but also for those who believe in me through their word,
that all may be one; that as you, Father, are in me and I in you, they also may be in us,{g} so that the world may believe that you sent me.
The glory that you have given me I have given to them, that they may be one as we are one,
I in them and you in me, that they may be brought to perfect oneness, so that the world may come to know that you sent me and loved them as you loved me.
Father, as for what you have given me,{h} I desire that where I am, they also may be with me, to behold my glory, which you have given me because you loved me before the foundation of the world.
Father, you who are righteous: though the world did not know you, I knew you, and these men have come to know that it was you who sent me.
To them I revealed your name, and I will go on revealing it, so that the love you had for me may be within them, and I myself within them.”

notes.text: All whom you have given him: literally “all that you have given him,” a neuter singular collective, as also in 17:24.
I have revealed your name: literally “I manifested your name,” that is, revealed who God is.

The name you have given me: so the Westcott–Hort text with the earliest manuscripts (the relative pronoun agreeing with “name”); some later manuscripts read “those whom you have given me.” So also in 17:12.
The son of destruction: a Semitic idiom for one destined to perish (compare 2 Thess 2:3), here Judas. The Scripture is probably Ps 41:9, quoted in 13:18.
From the evil one: or “from evil.”
Make them holy: Greek *hagiason*, “sanctify, consecrate, set apart for God”; the same verb is rendered “consecrate” in 17:19.
In us: many manuscripts read “one in us.”
What you have given me: see the note on 17:2. Many manuscripts read “those whom you have given me.”

verses.text: After saying these things, Jesus went out with his disciples across the Kidron ravine,{a} where there was a garden, which he and his disciples entered.
Judas, who was betraying him, also knew the place, for Jesus had often met there with his disciples.
So Judas, having taken the cohort{b} and some officers from the chief priests and from the Pharisees, comes there with lanterns and torches and weapons.
Then Jesus, knowing all that was about to befall him, came forward and says to them, “Whom are you seeking?”
They answered him, “Jesus the Nazarene.” He says to them, “I am he.”{c} Judas, who was betraying him, was also standing with them.
As soon as he told them, “I am he,” they stepped backward and dropped to the ground.
Again then he asked them, “Whom are you seeking?” And they said, “Jesus the Nazarene.”
“I have told you I am he,” Jesus replied. “If it is me you want, then allow these to go their way.”
This was to fulfill the word he had spoken, “Of those you have given me I have not lost one.”{d}
Simon Peter had a sword; he drew it, struck at the slave of the high priest, and sliced off his right ear. Malchus{e} was the slave’s name.
So Jesus said to Peter, “Put the sword into its sheath. The cup the Father has given me, shall I not drink it?”
Then the cohort and its commander{f} and the officers of the Jews seized Jesus and bound him.
They led him first to Annas,{g} for he was father-in-law of Caiaphas, who was high priest that year.
It was Caiaphas who had counseled the Jews that it was expedient for one man to die for the people.
Simon Peter followed Jesus, along with another disciple. Because this disciple was an acquaintance of the high priest, he went in with Jesus into the high priest’s courtyard,
but Peter was standing by the door outside. The other disciple, the acquaintance of the high priest, came out, had a word with the doorkeeper, and brought Peter inside.
The servant girl at the door then says to Peter, “You are not one of this man’s disciples too, are you?” He says, “I am not.”
The slaves and the officers had lit a charcoal fire, since it was cold, and stood about it warming themselves; and Peter too stood among them, warming himself.
The high priest therefore asked Jesus about his disciples and what he taught.
Jesus answered him, “I have spoken openly to the world. I always taught in synagogue and in the temple, where all the Jews come together, and in secret I said nothing.
Why do you ask me? Ask the people who heard what I told them. They know what I said.”
After he said this, one of the officers who was standing there slapped Jesus and said, “Is this how you respond to the high priest?”
Jesus answered him, “If I spoke wrongly, testify to the wrong; but if rightly, why do you strike me?”
Annas then sent him bound to Caiaphas the high priest.
Simon Peter, meanwhile, stood warming himself. They said to him, “Surely you are not another of his disciples?” He denied it: “I am not.”
A slave of the high priest, kinsman to the one whose ear Peter had cut off, says, “Didn’t I see you in the garden, with him?”
Again Peter denied it; and at once a rooster crowed.

From Caiaphas, then, they bring Jesus to the governor’s headquarters.{h} It was early morning.{i} They did not go into the headquarters themselves, lest they incur defilement; they wanted to eat the Passover.{j}
Pilate{k} therefore came out to them and says, “What accusation are you bringing against this man?”
They answered him, “If this man were not a wrongdoer, we would not have handed him over to you.”
“You take him,” Pilate said to them, “and try him under your own law.” The Jews told him, “We have no legal right to execute anyone.”{l}
This was to fulfill the word Jesus had spoken to indicate by what kind of death he was going to die.
Pilate went back inside the headquarters, called for Jesus, and asked him, “Are you the king of the Jews?”
Jesus replied, “Is this your own question, or did other people say this to you about me?”
Pilate replied, “Am I a Jew? Your own people and their chief priests handed you over to me. What did you do?”
“My kingdom is not of this world,” Jesus answered. “If it were, those who serve me would be fighting to prevent my being handed over to the Jews. But in fact my kingdom does not come from here.”

“So you are a king?” Pilate asked. Jesus answered, “You say that I am a king.{m} I was born for this, and for this I came into the world: to testify to the truth. Everyone who belongs to the truth hears my voice.”
Pilate says to him, “What is truth?” After saying this, he went out again to the Jews and says to them, “I find no case against him.
It is a custom of yours that I set someone free for you at the Passover. Would you like me, then, to set free for you the King of the Jews?”
They shouted back, “Not this man, but Barabbas!”{n} Now Barabbas was a bandit.{o}

notes.text: Kidron ravine: Greek *cheimarros*, a “winter torrent,” a valley that runs with water only in the rainy season, here the Kidron valley east of Jerusalem, between the city and the Mount of Olives.
Cohort: Greek *speira*, a Roman unit nominally of 600 soldiers, though here perhaps a detachment.
I am he: Greek *egō eimi*, “I am”; in context an identification, but see the notes on 6:20 and 8:58; the arresting party’s falling to the ground (18:6) suggests the fuller sense. So in 18:6, 8.
Malchus: a Semitic name, “king” or “counselor.”
Commander: Greek *chiliarchos*, “commander of a thousand,” a Roman military tribune.
Annas: high priest AD 6–15, still powerful afterward; five of his sons and his son-in-law Caiaphas held the office. *Annas* is a Greek form of Hebrew *Hanan*, “gracious.”
Governor’s headquarters: Greek *praitōrion*, the Roman governor’s residence (praetorium) in Jerusalem, probably Herod’s palace or the Antonia fortress.
Early morning: Greek *prōi*, the last watch of the night, about 3–6 a.m.

Eat the Passover: in John, Jesus is crucified on the day of preparation for the Passover (19:14, 31), at the time the lambs were slaughtered; in Matthew, Mark and Luke the Last Supper is a Passover meal. The relation of the two chronologies is much discussed.
Pilate: Pontius Pilate, Roman prefect of Judea AD 26–36.

We have no legal right to execute anyone: under Roman rule the Jewish authorities apparently lacked the right of capital punishment, at least for a case such as this. John 18:31–33 and 37–38 are preserved in P52 (John Rylands Library, Manchester), a small papyrus fragment usually dated about AD 125–175 and one of the oldest surviving New Testament manuscripts.
You say that I am a king: or “You say it: I am a king.” Compare Matt 27:11; Mark 15:2; Luke 23:3.
Barabbas: Aramaic, “son of the father” (or “son of Abba”). See Matt 27:16–17, where some manuscripts give his name as Jesus Barabbas.
Bandit: Greek *lēstēs*, a robber, often used by Josephus of armed insurgents against Rome.

verses.text: Pilate then took Jesus and had him flogged.{a}
The soldiers twisted thorns into a crown and set it upon his head, and threw a purple robe around him;
Again and again they came up to him with “Hail, King of the Jews!” and struck him in the face.
Pilate came outside once more and says to them, “Here, I am bringing him out to you, so you may know that I find no case against him.”
So out came Jesus, wearing the thorny crown and the purple robe. And Pilate says to them, “Look: the man!”{b}
At the sight of him the chief priests and the officers shouted, “Crucify, crucify!” Pilate tells them, “You take him and crucify him; I find no case against him.”
The Jews answered him, “We have a law, and by that law he ought to die, for he has made himself out to be God’s Son.”
When Pilate heard this statement, he grew more afraid than ever.
Then he went inside the headquarters again and said to Jesus, “Where have you come from?” But Jesus did not answer him.
So Pilate says to him, “Will you not speak to me? Do you not realize I have power to release you, and power to crucify you?”
“You would hold no authority over me at all,” Jesus answered, “unless it had been given you from above.{c} That is why the man who delivered me to you is guilty of a greater sin.”
After this Pilate tried to set him free, but the Jews cried out, “Set this man free, and you are no Friend of Caesar!{d} Whoever makes himself a king is defying Caesar.”
On hearing these words, Pilate brought Jesus outside and sat down{e} on the judgment seat at a place called the Stone Pavement, in Hebrew{f} Gabbatha.{g}
It was the day of Preparation for the Passover, about noon.{h} And he says to the Jews, “Here is your king!”
They shouted, “Away with him! Away with him! Crucify him!” Pilate says to them, “Shall I crucify your king?” The chief priests answered, “We have no king but Caesar.”
So then he delivered him up to them for crucifixion, and they took Jesus away.
He went out, bearing the cross on his own, to the spot known as Skull Place, Golgotha{i} in Hebrew.
They nailed him to the cross there, and two other men along with him, one on each side and Jesus between them.
Pilate also had a notice{j} written and fixed on the cross; it read, “JESUS THE NAZARENE, THE KING OF THE JEWS.”
Many of the Jews read this notice, because the place where Jesus was crucified was near the city; and it was written in Hebrew, in Latin, and in Greek.
The chief priests of the Jews said to Pilate, “Do not write, ‘The King of the Jews.’ Write instead that he claimed, ‘I am the King of the Jews.’”
Pilate answered, “What I have written, I have written.”

The soldiers, after crucifying Jesus, took his garments and divided them in four, one portion for each soldier. They took the tunic too; it had no seam, being woven in one piece throughout from the top.

They said to each other, “Let us not tear it. Instead, let us cast lots to see who will get it.” This was so that the Scripture would be fulfilled that says: “They shared out my clothes among them, and for my robe they cast lots.”{k} And that is what the soldiers did.
By the cross of Jesus there stood his mother, and his mother’s sister, Mary the wife of Clopas,{l} and Mary Magdalene.{m}
Jesus, seeing his mother and the disciple whom he loved standing near, says to his mother, “Woman,{n} here is your son.”
Next he says to the disciple, “Here is your mother.” From that hour on, the disciple received her into his own household.
After this, Jesus, knowing that all was now accomplished, says (so that the Scripture might be fulfilled), “I thirst.”{o}
A jar of sour wine{p} was sitting there. They soaked a sponge in the wine, fixed it on a branch of hyssop{q}, and lifted it to his mouth.
Having taken the sour wine, Jesus said, “It is finished”;{r} and he bowed his head and handed over his spirit.

Now it was the day of Preparation, and the Jews did not want the bodies left on the crosses over the Sabbath, especially as that Sabbath was a high day.{s} So they requested Pilate to have the men’s legs broken{t} and the bodies removed.
So the soldiers came and broke the legs of the first man, and then of the other who had been crucified with him.
But when they got to Jesus and saw that he had already died, they did not break his legs.
Instead, one of the soldiers pierced his side with a spear, and blood and water immediately flowed out.
The man who saw this has testified to it, and his testimony is true. He knows that he is telling the truth, so that you also may believe.
For these things took place to fulfill the Scripture, “Not one bone of his shall be broken.”{u}
And again another Scripture says, “They will look on him whom they pierced.”{v}

After this, Joseph of Arimathea,{w} who was a disciple of Jesus, though a secret one for fear of the Jews, asked Pilate whether he might remove the body of Jesus; and Pilate gave permission. So he came and removed his body.
Nicodemus came too, the man who had first come to Jesus by night, bringing a mixture{x} of myrrh and aloes, about seventy-five pounds.{y}
They took the body of Jesus and wrapped it in linen strips together with the spices, as is the Jewish custom of burial.
At the place where he was crucified there was a garden, and in the garden a new tomb in which no one had ever yet been laid.
So, because of the Jewish day of Preparation, and because the tomb was close at hand, they laid Jesus there.

notes.text: Flogged: Greek *mastigoō*, the Roman scourging with a whip of leather thongs weighted with bone or metal, often inflicted before crucifixion.
Look: the man!: or “Here is the man!” (Latin *Ecce homo*).
From above: that is, from God; the same Greek word as “again”/“from above” in 3:3, 7.
Friend of Caesar: perhaps an honorary title (Latin *amicus Caesaris*) for officials loyal to the emperor, here Tiberius (AD 14–37). *Caesar* became the imperial title.
Sat down: or “seated him” (that is, seated Jesus) on the judgment seat; the Greek can be read either way.
Hebrew: here and in 19:17, 20 probably meaning Aramaic, the everyday language of Jews in the land.
Gabbatha: an Aramaic name of uncertain meaning, perhaps “height” or “ridge.”

About noon: literally “about the sixth hour,” counting from about 6 a.m.; see the note on 1:39. If John reckoned from midnight, as has sometimes been proposed, the time would be about 6 a.m. Mark 15:25 places the crucifixion at the third hour (about 9 a.m.); the two accounts have been reconciled in various ways, and a few manuscripts read “third” here.
Golgotha: Aramaic *gulgulta*, “skull”; Latin *calvaria*, whence “Calvary.”
Notice: Greek *titlos* (Latin *titulus*), a placard stating the charge against the condemned.
Ps 22:18 (21:19 Greek), following the Greek Old Testament.

Mary the wife of Clopas: literally “Mary of Clopas,” perhaps “wife” or “daughter.” It is uncertain whether three or four women are named (his mother’s sister may be a separate person). *Clopas* may be the same as Cleopas (Luke 24:18).
Mary Magdalene: “Mary of Magdala,” a town on the west shore of the Sea of Galilee; *Magdala* means “tower.”
Woman: a respectful form of address (see the note on 2:4).
I thirst: compare Ps 22:15; 69:21.
Sour wine: Greek *oxos*, cheap wine vinegar, a common drink of soldiers and laborers.

Hyssop: a small bushy plant used to sprinkle the blood of the Passover lamb (Exod 12:22). Because its stalk is short, some have conjectured *hyssō*, “on a javelin,” a reading found in one late manuscript.
It is finished: Greek *tetelestai*, “it has been completed, accomplished”; the same verb as “accomplished” in 19:28.
High day: that Sabbath coincided with the Passover festival (see 19:14 and 18:28).
Have the men’s legs broken: breaking a crucified man’s legs (Latin *crurifragium*) hastened death by suffocation.
Exod 12:46; Num 9:12 (of the Passover lamb); compare Ps 34:20.
Zech 12:10, in a form closer to the Hebrew than to the Greek Old Testament.
Arimathea: a town in Judea, perhaps Ramathaim (1 Sam 1:1), about 20 miles (32 km) northwest of Jerusalem. *Joseph* means “may he add.”
Mixture: so the Westcott–Hort text with Sinaiticus (first hand) and Vaticanus (as reported, *heligma*, “package, roll”); most manuscripts read *migma*, “mixture.”

About seventy-five pounds: literally “about a hundred litras.” The Roman pound (*litra*, Latin *libra*) was about 12 ounces (327 g), so the total was about 75 pounds (33 kg), a quantity fit for a royal burial.

verses.text: On the first day of the week,{a} early, while it was still dark, Mary Magdalene comes to the tomb and sees that the stone has been taken away from the tomb.
She runs, then, and comes to Simon Peter and the other disciple, whom Jesus held dear, and says to them, “They have removed the Lord from the tomb, and where they have laid him we cannot tell!”
Peter therefore set out with the other disciple, and they made for the tomb.
The two were running side by side, but the other disciple outran Peter and was first to arrive at the tomb.
Stooping to look in, he sees the linen strips lying there; he did not, however, go in.
Then Simon Peter arrives, following him, and he went into the tomb. He looks at the linen strips lying there,
and the face cloth that had been on his head, not lying with the strips but rolled up in a place by itself.
Then the other disciple, who had reached the tomb first, went in as well, and he saw and believed;
They did not yet grasp the Scripture that he had to rise again out of death.
The disciples then went back home again.
But Mary stayed outside by the tomb, weeping. As she wept, she bent down to look into the tomb,
and she sees two angels in white sitting where the body of Jesus had lain, one at the head and one at the feet.
“Woman,” they say to her, “what are you weeping for?” She tells them, “Someone has removed my Lord, and where they have laid him I cannot tell.”
On saying this she turned around, and she sees Jesus standing there, but she did not know that it was Jesus.

Jesus says to her, “Woman, why are you weeping? Whom are you looking for?” She, supposing him to be the gardener, says to him, “Sir, if it was you who carried him off, tell me where you put him, and I will take him away.”
Jesus says to her, “Mary.” She turns and says to him in Hebrew, “Rabbouni!”{b} (which means Teacher).

Jesus told her, “Do not cling to me,{c} since I have not yet ascended to the Father. Rather, go to my brothers and give them this message: ‘I am going up to my Father, who is also your Father, to my God, who is also your God.’”
Mary Magdalene goes and announces to the disciples, “I have seen the Lord,” and that he had told her these things.

When evening came on that day, the first day of the week, and the doors of the place where the disciples were had been locked for fear of the Jews, Jesus came and stood among them and says to them, “Peace be with you.”
And after saying this he showed them his hands and his side. The disciples were overjoyed at seeing the Lord.
So Jesus said to them again, “Peace be with you. As the Father has sent me, so I am sending you.”
Having said this, he breathed on them{d} and says to them, “Receive the Holy Spirit.
If you forgive anyone’s sins, they stand forgiven; if you retain anyone’s, they stand retained.”
Thomas, however, one of the Twelve, the one called the Twin,{e} had been absent when Jesus came.

So the other disciples told him, “We have seen the Lord.” But he said to them, “I will never believe unless I see the nail marks in his hands, touch those marks with my finger, and put my hand into his side.”
Eight days later{f} his disciples were again indoors, and Thomas was with them. Though the doors were locked, Jesus comes and stood among them and said, “Peace be with you.”
Then he said to Thomas, “Put your finger here and look at my hands. Reach out your hand and place it in my side. Do not be unbelieving,{g} but believe.”
Thomas answered him, “My Lord and my God!”{h}
Jesus says to him, “Because you have seen me, you have believed? Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed.”
Now Jesus did many other signs in the presence of the disciples, which are not written in this book;
These, though, have been written that you may believe{i} Jesus to be the Messiah, God’s Son, and that through believing you may have life by his name.

notes.text: The first day of the week: literally “on the first of the sabbaths,” that is, of the week; our Sunday.
Rabbouni: an Aramaic form of “Rabbi,” literally “my master,” “my teacher.”
Stop clinging to me: or “Do not hold on to me”; the present imperative suggests stopping an action already begun. The older rendering “Touch me not” is from the Latin *Noli me tangere*.
Breathed on them: Greek *enephysēsen*, the verb used in the Greek Old Testament of God breathing life into the first man (Gen 2:7) and in Ezek 37:9.
Twin: see the note on 11:16.
Eight days later: counting inclusively, the following Sunday.
Stop doubting: literally “Do not be unbelieving, but believing.”
My Lord and my God: compare 1:1, 18. *Lord and God* was a combination used of the God of Israel in the Greek Old Testament (for example Ps 35:23).

May believe: so the Westcott–Hort text with P66 (apparently), Sinaiticus (first hand) and Vaticanus (as reported), a present tense that may mean “continue to believe”; most manuscripts read the aorist, which may mean “come to believe.” Many scholars regard 20:30–31 as the original ending of the Gospel, with chapter 21 an epilogue; no manuscript lacks chapter 21.

verses.text: Later, Jesus again made himself known to the disciples beside the Sea of Tiberias.{a} This is how he made himself known.
Simon Peter, Thomas (known as the Twin), Nathanael of Cana in Galilee, the sons of Zebedee,{b} and two other disciples of Jesus were together.
Simon Peter says to them, “I am going fishing.” They say to him, “We will come with you.” They went out and got into the boat, and that night they caught nothing.
At daybreak Jesus was standing on the beach, but the disciples did not realize that it was Jesus.
So Jesus says to them, “Lads,{c} you have no fish to eat, have you?” They answered him, “No.”
He said to them, “Cast the net on the right-hand side of the boat, and you will find some.” So they cast it, and now they could not haul it in for the great number of fish.

The disciple whom Jesus loved said to Peter, “It is the Lord!” When Simon Peter heard that it was the Lord, he wrapped his outer garment around himself (he had been working without it) and jumped into the sea.
The other disciples followed in the small boat, pulling the net full of fish, since they were not far from shore, only about a hundred yards.{d}
When they got out onto the land, they see a charcoal fire laid there, with fish lying on it, and bread.
Jesus says to them, “Bring some of the fish you have just caught.”
Simon Peter therefore climbed up and dragged the net to land, crammed with big fish, one hundred fifty-three{e} in all; and for all their number, the net did not split.
“Come and eat,” says Jesus to them. Not one of the disciples ventured to inquire, “Who are you?” for they knew it was the Lord.
Jesus comes and takes the bread and gives it to them, and the fish likewise.
That made the third time Jesus appeared to the disciples after rising from the dead.

When they had eaten breakfast, Jesus says to Simon Peter, “Simon son of John,{f} do you love me more than these?”{g} He says to him, “Yes, Lord; you know that I love you.”{h} He says to him, “Feed my lambs.”
He says to him again, a second time, “Simon son of John, do you love me?” He says to him, “Yes, Lord; you know that I love you.” He says to him, “Shepherd my sheep.”

A third time he says to him, “Simon son of John, do you love me?” It hurt Peter that he asked him a third time, “Do you love me?” and he answered, “Lord, you know everything; you are aware that I love you.” Jesus says to him, “Feed my sheep.

Amen, amen, I tell you, in your youth you put on your own belt and went about where you pleased; but when you have grown old, you will stretch out your hands,{i} and someone else will belt you and lead you where you would not go.”
He said this to show the kind of death by which Peter would bring glory to God. Then he told him, “Follow me.”
Peter turned and sees the disciple whom Jesus loved following them, the one who had leaned back against his chest at the supper and said, “Lord, who is it that is betraying you?”
Seeing him, Peter says to Jesus, “Lord, and what about him?”
Jesus says to him, “Suppose I wish him to stay until I come; what concern is that of yours? As for you, follow me.”

Hence the report went out among the brothers that this disciple was not going to die. But Jesus had not said to him that he would not die; only, “Suppose I wish him to stay until I come; what concern is that of yours?”
This is the disciple who bears witness about these things and who has written them, and we know that his witness is true.{j}
Jesus did many other things besides. Were they to be written down one by one, I imagine the world itself would not have room for the books that would be written.{k}

notes.text: Sea of Tiberias: the Sea of Galilee (see the note on 6:1).
The sons of Zebedee: James and John, mentioned only here in this Gospel. *Zebedee* is from Hebrew, “gift (of Yahweh).”
Lads: Greek *paidia*, “children,” a familiar form of address.
About a hundred yards: literally “about two hundred cubits,” about 300 feet (90 m).
One hundred fifty-three: many symbolic interpretations have been proposed (for example, Jerome reported that Greek zoologists counted 153 kinds of fish), but none is certain.
Simon son of John: so the Westcott–Hort text with Sinaiticus and Vaticanus (as reported); many manuscripts read “Simon son of Jonah,” as in Matt 16:17. So in 21:16, 17. See the note on 1:42.
More than these: either “more than these others do” or “more than you love these things.”

Love … love: in 21:15–17 Jesus twice asks with *agapaō* and the third time with *phileō*, while Peter answers each time with *phileō*. Many interpreters see the change as stylistic variation, since John uses both verbs of the same love (compare 3:35 and 5:20); others find a deliberate distinction.
Stretch out your hands: early Christian writers took this as a reference to crucifixion; tradition holds that Peter was crucified in Rome under Nero, about AD 64–67.
We know that his witness is true: the “we” appears to be a group associated with the beloved disciple who vouch for his testimony; see the note on 13:23.
The books that would be written: in the manuscripts of family 1 (as reported), the account of the woman caught in adultery (7:53–8:11) is placed after this verse; see the note on 7:53.
